subject: MGMT464
title: Hurdle 5 · The Mutiny Camp — Influencing: Power, Politics, Networking and Negotiation

questions.stem: Describe position power.
options: Authority delegated down the chain of command — anyone appointed to the position gets it and loses it on leaving
Power derived from the followers, based on the leader's behaviour, expertise and relationships with them over time
Power from physical strength and the ability to force others to do what the leader wants
Power from money only — the ability to pay people and reward them for what they do
questions.why: Legitimate, reward, coercive and connection come mainly from position. See §5.1.

questions.stem: Describe personal power.
options: Derived from the followers, based on the leader's expertise, character and relationships — it travels with the person
Derived from the job title and the formal authority that the organisation attaches to the position, whoever happens to hold it at the time
Delegated from top management down the chain of command to whoever holds the post
Lost on leaving the position, because it belongs to the role rather than to the person
questions.why: Expert, information and referent power. See §5.1.

questions.stem: Explain the textbook's key point about the two kinds of power.
options: Position power gets compliance; personal power gets commitment — use position power sparingly and build personal power continuously
Position power is always better, because it does not depend on whether the followers happen to like or respect the leader at the time
Personal power is illegal in most organisations, because it bypasses the formal chain of command
Only one kind can be held at a time, so the leader must choose between position and personal power
questions.why: Personal power is what remains when followers can choose. See §5.1.

questions.stem: Explain why Mark Cuban's problems arise, in the chapter's reading.
options: He used coercive and position power where personal power was needed — with referees and the league he does not command
He has no power at all over the game, because the league, the referees and the other owners are completely outside his organisation
He never uses position power, so his players and staff do not take his authority seriously
He lacks expertise in basketball and so cannot build the expert power a team owner needs
questions.why: Answer to question 1. See §5.1.

questions.stem: Identify the seven types of power.
options: Legitimate, reward, coercive, referent, expert, information, connection
Rational, emotional, legal, moral, social, financial, physical
Trait, behaviour, contingency, charisma, culture, strategy, team
Decide, consult, facilitate, delegate, direct, support, achieve and reward
questions.why: French and Raven's five extended to seven. See §5.2.

questions.stem: Describe referent power.
options: Relationships and personal traits — people like and identify with the leader
The ability to punish followers who do not comply with the leader's requests
Control over data and information that other people need to do their work
The authority of the position, which followers accept because of the title
questions.why: Referent — personal. See §5.2.

questions.stem: Identify how the textbook says to use coercive power.
options: Rarely and as a last resort — it destroys personal power
Daily, to keep order and make sure that followers take the leader seriously
Only in public, so that the whole team learns the lesson at once
Never, under any circumstances, because punishment is always unethical
questions.why: Coercive. See §5.2.

questions.stem: Explain the chapter's UAE test for a young manager of a multinational team.
options: Legitimate power is respected, but expert and referent power are what make the team follow — build the personal three first
Only legitimate power matters, because a multinational team respects the hierarchy above everything else and expects to be told what to do
Coercive power works best, because a young manager must show the team who is in charge from the start
Connection power is enough, because a young manager with the right contacts will be obeyed
questions.why: The UAE test. See §5.2.

questions.stem: Identify the nine influencing tactics.
options: Rational persuasion, inspirational appeal, consultation, ingratiation, personal appeal, exchange, coalition, legitimisation, pressure
Decide, consult individually, consult group, facilitate, delegate, direct, support, participate, achieve and coach — the ten styles from the earlier chapters
Plan, negotiate, postpone, agree, network, reciprocate, build coalitions, praise, punish
Trait, behaviour, situation, power, politics, networking, negotiation, ethics, culture
questions.why: Nine ways to turn power into influence. See §5.3.

questions.stem: Describe rational persuasion and the power it uses.
options: Logical arguments and factual evidence — expert and information power
Appeal to the person's values and ideals — referent power
Demands and threats to make the person comply — coercive power
Pointing to the rules and the authority of the position — legitimate power
questions.why: Works when the person cares about the facts. See §5.3.

questions.stem: Identify the tactic that costs personal power every time.
options: Pressure
Consultation
Rational persuasion
Inspirational appeal
questions.why: A last resort. See §5.3.

questions.stem: Explain the chapter's answer to why one colleague was promoted and the equally competent one was not.
options: The promoted person used rational persuasion, consultation and coalition — building agreement before the decision; work does not speak, people do
Luck — the two colleagues were equally competent and the decision could have gone either way on the day, whatever either of them did or said in the meeting
The promoted person was related to the boss, which is the usual reason in organisations of that kind
The other colleague was lazy and did not deserve the promotion whatever the influence tactics used
questions.why: Answer to question 2. See §5.3.

questions.stem: Describe the textbook's reframe of politics.
options: Like money, politics is a medium of exchange — neither good nor bad in itself; how it is used matters
Politics is always corrupt, and the ethical manager stays out of it entirely and lets the quality of the work speak for itself
Politics is only for politicians, and managers who play it have forgotten what their job is
Politics replaces work in organisations where the formal systems have broken down
questions.why: Politics is the process of gaining and using power. See §5.4.

questions.stem: Identify the three kinds of political behaviour.
options: Networking, reciprocity and coalition
Lying, bribing and threatening
Planning, organising and controlling
Praise, pressure and the exchange of favours
questions.why: All three are ethical when the objective is legitimate and the exchange is honest. See §5.4.

questions.stem: Explain why politics exists in organisations.
options: Limited resources, competing goals and ambiguous decisions — where rules do not decide, people do
Because managers are dishonest by nature and prefer informal deals to the formal procedures of the organisation
Because government rules require organisations to consult before deciding
Because of social media, which makes every decision visible and contestable
questions.why: The informal organisation runs beside the formal one. See §5.4.

questions.stem: Explain the chapter's answer to 'can I refuse to play politics?'.
options: You cannot refuse to play; you can only choose to play badly — your good ideas lose to worse ideas that were better supported
Yes, refuse and succeed anyway, because results are what organisations reward in the end and politics is a distraction from the work
Yes, if your work is good enough, because excellent work is noticed without any support
No, because politics is illegal and refusing to take part would be a breach of your duties
questions.why: Answer to question 3. See §5.4.

questions.stem: Identify the most important political relationship, according to the textbook.
options: Your manager — deliver, keep them informed, give no surprises
Your competitor for the next promotion, who must be watched closely
The receptionist, who knows everything that happens in the building
Your best friend at work, who will support you in every meeting
questions.why: Develop good working relationships. See §5.5.

questions.stem: Identify an unethical political behaviour from the chapter's table.
options: Undermining rivals or withholding information
Building genuine relationships with people across the organisation
Fair exchange where both sides gain something they value
Sharing credit for results with the people who helped produce them
questions.why: Ethical vs unethical. See §5.5.

questions.stem: Identify the textbook's ethical test for politics.
options: Would you be comfortable if the way you gained support were public?
Did you win the decision in the end?
Did your manager approve of the way you went about gaining the support?
Was it fast enough to meet the deadline?
questions.why: The textbook's test, and Chapter 2's. See §5.5.

questions.stem: Describe the guideline 'gain recognition — and be a team player'.
options: Let results be known, take visible projects, give credit to others and never take it; help people before you need them
Hide your results until the annual review so that nobody can claim them, and keep your projects to yourself until they are finished
Take credit for team work, because the leader is responsible for the team's results
Avoid visible projects, because they carry the risk of visible failure
questions.why: Reciprocity. See §5.5.

questions.stem: Identify the six steps of the networking process.
options: Self-assessment and goals; one-minute self-sell; develop your network; networking interviews; maintain your network; follow up
Plan the meeting carefully; negotiate the terms; postpone if needed; agree; write the agreement down; keep the agreement and follow up
Find a vacancy; apply; interview; accept the offer; start work; leave for the next job
Post regularly; like others' posts; share content; comment; follow influencers; block critics
questions.why: Six steps. See §5.6.

questions.stem: Identify the three parts of the one-minute self-sell.
options: History, plans, and a question that invites help
Name, current salary and hobbies
The problem, the proposed solution and the asking price
Strengths, weaknesses and threats
questions.why: Sixty seconds, rehearsed. See §5.6.

questions.stem: Describe what a networking interview asks for.
options: Twenty minutes of advice, not a job — plus two more names
A job offer or at least an interview for a vacancy
A salary figure for the role you are interested in
A reference letter from someone senior in the field you want to enter
questions.why: Conduct networking interviews. See §5.6.

questions.stem: Explain why most people's networking fails.
options: They network only when they need something — exactly when it does not work
They have too many contacts and cannot maintain relationships with all of them
They use LinkedIn instead of meeting people face to face
They follow up too quickly and seem desperate
questions.why: Build it before it is needed. See §5.6.

questions.stem: Identify the three negotiation phases.
options: Plan; negotiate; postpone, then agree or not
Attack first, defend the position, then retreat
Open, close and sign
Ask, demand, threaten and then agree
questions.why: The textbook's model. See §5.7.

questions.stem: Identify the three objectives to set in the planning phase.
options: A specific limit (walk-away), a target, and an opening
A wish, a hope and a dream
Minimum, maximum and average pay
A first offer, a second offer and a third and final offer
questions.why: Most negotiations are won or lost in the planning. See §5.7.

questions.stem: Describe a BATNA.
options: Your best alternative if there is no agreement — the person with an alternative is never desperate
The first offer you make, which sets the anchor for the rest of the negotiation and signals your confidence
The final price agreed by both sides at the end of the negotiation
A written contract signed by both parties once agreement is reached
questions.why: Know your alternative. See §5.7.

questions.stem: Explain why the negotiation in question 4 went badly.
options: There was no plan — no limit, no target, no alternative
The other side was rude and refused to negotiate in good faith
The room was cold and the meeting was held at the wrong time of day
The price was too low for the other side to accept
questions.why: Answer to question 4. See §5.7.

questions.stem: Describe how negotiation connects to the rest of the chapter.
options: Negotiation is conflict handled through influence; tactics are how power is used; politics is where it happens
Negotiation is unrelated to power, because it depends entirely on the quality of the arguments each side presents
Negotiation replaces politics, because an agreement removes the need for informal influence
Negotiation needs no tactics, because both sides want to reach an agreement
questions.why: One map. See §5.8.

questions.stem: Identify the ethical test for influencing tactics.
options: Would the person accept the tactic if they saw it named?
Did it work and produce the result you wanted?
Was it fast enough to meet the deadline?
Was it legal under the organisation's rules and the law of the country?
questions.why: Ethics runs through every box. See §5.8.

questions.stem: Describe the consultation tactic.
options: Ask the person to help plan or improve the idea — for commitment, not only compliance
Offer the person something they value in return for their agreement, and make sure the exchange is kept
Point to your authority or the organisation's rules
Praise the person before making the request
questions.why: Referent and expert power. See §5.3.

questions.stem: Identify how to increase expert power.
options: Keep learning; become the expert in your area; share it
Get control over the resources that others need
Network deliberately with the people who hold power
Take on more responsibility so that your position grows
questions.why: Expert — personal. See §5.2.

questions.stem: Exercise 1A: a nurse manager persuades the hospital to buy new monitors by presenting six months of incident data. Classify the tactic and the power.
options: Rational persuasion — expert and information power
Coalition — connection power with the senior doctors
Pressure — coercive power
Legitimisation — legitimate power
questions.why: Answer key: A rational persuasion / expert + information. See §5.3 and Exercise 1.

questions.stem: Exercise 1B: a project lead asks two respected senior engineers to back her proposal before the meeting, so the director hears three voices. Classify the tactic, the power, and whether it is ethical.
options: Coalition — connection power; political, and ethical if the proposal is legitimate and the seniors agree on merit
Ingratiation — referent power; unethical because she flatters the senior engineers into supporting a proposal they have not examined
Pressure — coercive power; unethical because the director is forced to agree
Exchange — reward power; ethical because the seniors receive something in return
questions.why: Answer key: B coalition / connection — ethical on merit. See §5.3, §5.5 and Exercise 1.

questions.stem: Exercise 1C: a supervisor reminds a late employee that policy requires a written warning after the third late arrival. Classify the tactic and the power.
options: Legitimisation — legitimate power
Pressure — coercive power
Rational persuasion — expert power
Personal appeal — referent power
questions.why: Answer key: C legitimisation / legitimate. See §5.3 and Exercise 1.

questions.stem: Exercise 1D: a team leader invites a sceptical colleague to help redesign the plan he opposed; the colleague becomes its champion. Classify the tactic and the power.
options: Consultation — referent and expert power
Ingratiation — referent power and flattery
Coalition — connection power and allies
Exchange — reward power
questions.why: Answer key: D consultation / referent + expert. See §5.3 and Exercise 1.

questions.stem: Exercise 1E: a manager threatens to cancel a technician's leave unless the report is finished tonight. Determine the tactic, its cost, and the rewrite.
options: Pressure — coercive power; costs referent power; rewrite as exchange: 'the client needs it by 9 a.m.; if you can finish tonight I will cover your Thursday shift'
Exchange — reward power; fair because the technician's leave is the manager's to grant and the manager is being generous with it; keep the message exactly as it is written
Legitimisation — legitimate power; the manager is entitled to set deadlines; keep it as it is
Consultation — referent power; the manager is asking the technician for ideas; keep it as it is
questions.why: Answer key: E pressure / coercive — rewrite as exchange. See §5.3 and Exercise 1.

questions.stem: Exercise 1F: a young analyst asks a mentor for 20 minutes of advice on moving into strategy — and for two more names. Classify the behaviour and the power it builds.
options: A networking interview — connection power; political and ethical
Pressure — coercive power; the analyst is forcing the mentor's time
Legitimisation — legitimate power; the analyst is using the mentor's position
Ingratiation — referent power; the analyst is flattering the mentor
questions.why: Answer key: F networking interview / connection. See §5.6 and Exercise 1.

questions.stem: Determine which two Exercise 1 cases are political behaviour.
options: B (coalition) and F (networking)
A (rational persuasion) and C
D (consultation) and E (pressure)
C and E (pressure)
questions.why: Answer key, task 3. See §5.4 and Exercise 1.

questions.stem: Exercise 2: Noura, four months into a government entity, has pilot workload data and a simpler template but no authority over anyone. Determine the power she has and lacks.
options: Has expert and information power and some referent power with the supervisors; lacks legitimate, reward, coercive and connection power
Has legitimate and coercive power from her post as analyst in the director's office; lacks expert power because she is new to the organisation and to the field
Has all seven kinds of power because she has the pilot data
Has none of the seven kinds of power because she has no authority
questions.why: Marking guide, task 1. See §5.2 and Exercise 2.

questions.stem: Determine the two kinds of power Noura can build in the next month, and how.
options: Connection power (the supervisors, the director's assistant) and referent power (deliver, help)
Coercive and legitimate power — by asking the director for a promotion to a post with formal authority
Reward power — by buying lunches for the field teams
None — she must wait a year before any power is available to her
questions.why: Marking guide, task 1. See §5.2 and Exercise 2.

questions.stem: Select the three-tactic sequence from the marking guide for Noura's influence plan.
options: Consultation with the manager ('help me test whether the pilot data is representative'), then rational persuasion with the data, then coalition with two supervisors who volunteer their experience

Pressure on the manager to change the template, then legitimisation through the director's instructions, then exchange of favours with the supervisors to secure their support for the new version before the next review
Coalition with the supervisors first, then pressure on the manager with their support, then ingratiation to repair the relationship
Personal appeal to the director as a friend of her family, then pressure on the manager through the director's authority
questions.why: Marking guide, task 2. See §5.3 and Exercise 2.

questions.stem: Determine why pressure and legitimisation are not available to Noura.
options: Both need position power — coercive or legitimate — and she has no authority over anyone
They are unethical for everyone in every situation, whatever the objective, and the chapter says they should never be used by anyone
They take too long to produce results in a four-month post
Her manager has forbidden their use in the department
questions.why: Marking guide, task 2. See §5.3 and Exercise 2.

questions.stem: Determine whether Noura's coalition with two supervisors passes the ethical test.
options: Yes — a legitimate objective (the director's data on time) and an honest exchange; she would be comfortable if it were public
No — coalitions are always manipulation of the decision-maker, whatever the objective, because they replace argument with numbers
No — she lacks the authority to form a coalition
Yes — because she will win the argument with their support
questions.why: Marking guide, task 2. See §5.5 and Exercise 2.

questions.stem: Noura gets 15 minutes with her manager. Select her limit, target and opening from the marking guide.
options: Limit: the pilot data is reviewed by someone; target: a two-week trial of the simpler template; opening: a joint review of the workload figures
Limit: the template is scrapped completely and never used again; target: her promotion to team lead within the year; opening: a formal complaint to the director about the manager
Limit: nothing; target: nothing; opening: an apology for raising the issue
Limit: a pay rise; target: a new manager; opening: a threat to resign
questions.why: Marking guide, task 3. See §5.7 and Exercise 2.

questions.stem: Select the sentence Noura uses to focus on the obstacle, not the person.
options: 'We both want the director to get the data on time; the obstacle is the field time this version takes.'
'Your template is the problem, everyone in the field knows it, and the director will find out soon enough if it is not changed.'
'The director will blame you if the data is late again.'
'I know more about this than you do, so please listen.'
questions.why: Marking guide, task 3. See §5.7 and Exercise 2.

questions.stem: Select the trade-off Noura can offer in the negotiation.
options: She does the extra analysis herself
She resigns if the template is not changed
She reports the manager to the director
She copies the director on every email
questions.why: Marking guide: trade — she does the extra analysis. See §5.7 and Exercise 2.

questions.stem: The manager says no. Determine Noura's BATNA and how she keeps the relationship and the idea alive.
options: Alternative: propose a formal pilot through the director's review meeting; accept the manager's decision for now and offer to monitor the workload
Go over his head immediately to the director with the pilot data and ask the director to overrule the manager in front of the team at the next meeting
Drop the idea forever and use the manager's template
Tell the field teams to refuse the template until it is changed
questions.why: Marking guide, task 4. See §5.8 and Exercise 2.

questions.stem: Take-away: a student's self-sell is 'I'm a student and I need a job, do you have one?'. Determine what is missing.
options: History, plans and a question that invites help — and it asks for a job instead of advice
Nothing — it is direct and honest about what the student wants
A salary figure, so that the contact knows what the student expects
A longer speech explaining the student's qualifications, grades and work experience in detail
questions.why: History, plans, a question — and ask for advice, not a job. See §5.6 and the take-away.

questions.stem: Take-away: the conversation goes well and the student gets two names. Determine the step the textbook says must happen within 24 hours.
options: Follow up — a note within 24 hours, then a reason to stay in touch
Ask for a job now that the relationship is warm and the contact is in a good mood
Post about the meeting on social media
Wait a month before writing so as not to seem desperate for help
questions.why: Step 6. See §5.6 and the take-away.

questions.stem: Omar refuses to go on. Rami says 'I am the captain — you will march.' Omar marches, slowly, and sulks for two days. Determine the kind of power used and what it bought.
options: Position power — compliance, not commitment
Personal power — commitment to the mission
Referent power — loyalty to Rami
Expert power — respect for Rami's judgement
questions.why: Position power gets compliance. See §5.1.

questions.stem: Instead, Rami asks Omar to help plan the climb; Omar redesigns the route and leads it. Classify the tactic.
options: Consultation — referent and expert power
Pressure — coercive power
Legitimisation — legitimate power
Exchange — reward power and the promise of reciprocity
questions.why: Consultation gets commitment. See §5.3.

questions.stem: Dana tells Omar: 'Layla taught your sister to read. Remember that when you look at the fortress.' Classify the tactic.
options: Inspirational appeal — referent power
Rational persuasion — expert and information power
Coalition — connection power
Legitimisation — legitimate power
questions.why: Appeal to values and ideals. See §5.3.

questions.stem: Rami bargains with the boatman: he knows his limit (no more than two days' food), his target (passage tonight) and his alternative (the old bridge). Determine why he negotiates well.
options: He planned — limit, target, opening and a BATNA; a person with an alternative is never desperate
He shouted louder than the boatman and kept shouting until the boatman finally gave in and agreed to take the party across the river
He paid whatever was asked so that the party could cross tonight
He lied about the gang so that the boatman would be afraid to refuse
questions.why: Most negotiations are won in the planning. See §5.7.

questions.stem: Noor builds friendships with the village elders weeks before the party needs horses; when the day comes, the horses are ready. Classify the political behaviour.
options: Networking and reciprocity — relationships built before they are needed
Pressure on the elders to provide horses
Coercion of the villagers through their fear of the gang and of what Rami might do
Legitimisation through Rami's title as captain
questions.why: Build it before it is needed. See §5.4 and §5.6.

questions.stem: The Crow chief wins support by hiding information from his own lieutenants and taking credit for their raids. Classify using the ethics table.
options: Unethical political behaviour — withholding information and credit taken
Ethical — results are what count in a gang, and the chief delivers them every season
Ethical — he is the leader and the raids are his
Neutral — all leaders manage information
questions.why: Ethical vs unethical table. See §5.5.

questions.stem: Determine the power Noor holds when she alone knows which gang patrols pass at which hour.
options: Information power
Legitimate power from her position
Coercive power
Reward power
questions.why: Access to and control over data others need. See §5.2.

questions.stem: Rami uses the same persuasion with Omar as with the Crow chief and fails with one of them. Determine the chapter's lesson.
options: Choose the tactic that fits the person and the request — the same person can earn two ethical grades depending on the tactic
Tactics never matter in the end; only the leader's power decides whether influence works, and the chief has more power than Rami
Persuasion always works if the arguments are good enough
Only coercion works on villains, so Rami should threaten the chief
questions.why: The tactic decides. See §5.8 and §5.3.

questions.stem: Identify the ethical test for politics in the chapter's closing map.
options: Is the exchange honest and the objective legitimate?
Did you win the decision in the end?
Was it fast enough to meet the deadline?
Was it kept secret from the people it affected until it was decided?
questions.why: One map. See §5.8.

questions.stem: Identify the ethical test for negotiation.
options: Does the other side gain too? Is the agreement kept?
Did you get everything you asked for?
Was the other side desperate enough to accept the first offer?
Was it quick enough to save time for both sides?
questions.why: Ethics runs through every box. See §5.8.

questions.stem: Analyse the chapter's reading of Mark Cuban's two kinds of power. Determine the position sources and personal sources.
options: Position: owner — legitimate, reward, coercive; personal: self-made entrepreneur — expert, referent
Position: expert and information power; personal: coercive and reward power, because he can fine and bonus the players himself
Position: referent and connection; personal: legitimate and reward
Position: none, because he owns the team; personal: all seven kinds
questions.why: Answer to question 1. See §5.1.

questions.stem: Rami holds no title in the second village, yet its people do what he asks because of his record and his fairness. Classify the power.
options: Personal power — it travels with the person
Position power from his rank as captain of the party
Coercive power from the fear of the gang
Legitimate power from the village council
questions.why: Derived from the followers. See §5.1.

questions.stem: Rami is made chief of the village council and starts giving orders only; within a month, people obey slowly and share nothing. Determine the chapter's warning.
options: He is spending position power and not building personal power — compliance, not commitment
Position power is enough for a village chief, so the problem must lie with the villagers themselves
He needs more rules so that the villagers know exactly what is expected
He needs coercive power to punish those who obey slowly
questions.why: Use position power sparingly; build personal power continuously. See §5.1.

questions.stem: Rami is the only one who can read the gang's cipher. Classify the power and how to increase it.
options: Expert power — keep learning and share it
Coercive power — punish those who cannot read it
Legitimate power — get the title of chief cryptographer
Reward power — control who sees the messages
questions.why: Expert — personal. See §5.2.

questions.stem: Dana trades favours with the ferrymen — she minds their boats, they tell her the gang's crossings. Classify the political behaviour.
options: Reciprocity — creating obligations and alliances to accomplish objectives
Coercion of the ferrymen through threats of what the captain would do to them if they refused to carry the party across the river
Legitimisation through Rami's authority
Pressure on the ferrymen to share information
questions.why: Reciprocity. See §5.4.

questions.stem: Omar says 'I refuse to play politics; my scouting speaks for itself' — and his route is rejected for a worse one. Determine the chapter's verdict.
options: You cannot refuse to play; you can only play badly — work does not speak, people do
He is right — good scouting will be recognised in the end by anyone who looks at the results
Politics is unethical, so Omar is right to refuse
His route was worse, which is why it was rejected
questions.why: Answer to question 3. See §5.4.

questions.stem: Noor delivers every task Rami gives her, keeps him informed and never surprises him; in a crisis he trusts her first. Classify the guideline she follows.
options: Develop a good working relationship with your manager — deliver, inform, no surprises
Gain recognition for her work in front of the team and the director as early as possible in the four months
Learn who the power players are and stay close to them
Build a coalition of followers who support her
questions.why: Your manager is your most important political relationship. See §5.5.

questions.stem: Dana takes credit for the plan Noor drew. Classify the behaviour by the chapter's table and its cost.
options: Unethical — credit taken; it destroys trust and referent power
Ethical — results matter far more than who drew the plan in the first place
Neutral — the plan belongs to the whole party
Ethical — she presented it, so the credit is hers
questions.why: Credit shared vs credit taken. See §5.5.

questions.stem: Omar writes to a famous tracker only when he needs a map; the tracker never replies. Determine the networking rule broken.
options: Maintain the network — a contact you only call when you need something is not a contact
Create a short self-sell so that the tracker knows who Omar is, what he has done and what he is planning to do next
Set goals for what the network should deliver
Follow up within 24 hours of the first letter
questions.why: Maintain your network. See §5.6.

questions.stem: Rami wins the boatman's agreement but humiliates him in front of his crew; the next crossing costs double. Determine the ethical test failed.
options: The negotiation test — the other side must gain too, and the relationship kept
The power test — Rami used coercive power on the boatman in front of the crew
The networking test — Rami did not maintain the relationship with the boatman after the crossing
The tactic test — the boatman would not accept the tactic if named
questions.why: Does the other side gain too? See §5.8.

questions.stem: Determine the resource every tactic and negotiation draws on, according to the chapter's map.
options: Power — potential influence
Money to pay for what is needed
Time to build the relationships
Charisma that makes people want to agree
questions.why: Power is the resource. See §5.8.
